# Draft:Mayer jewelry dynasty

The Mayer jewellery dynasty is a German–Swiss family of jewellers, silversmiths, enamel artists, watch retailers and gemstone traders whose activities span more than 250 years. Originating in Haigerloch and later active in Pforzheim, Lucerne and Montreux, the dynasty founded or shaped five notable jewellery and watch firms by seven siblings around 1900: Victor Mayer, Meyle & Mayer, Leicht-Mayer, Albert Mayer and Roman Mayer. Through these houses the family helped define German Jugendstil (Art Nouveau) jewellery, built a network of luxury watch boutiques across Swiss resorts, and – via the Pforzheim manufacture Victor Mayer – became one of the key producers of modern Fabergé jewellery under the label Fabergé Paris and later under Fabergé licences.
Origins
The Christian line of the family traces its origins to Uri Kitzinger (c. 1720–1754), a Jewish merchant in Haigerloch who converted in 1754 under the baptismal name Meinrad Kizinger. His descendants settled in the County of Hohenzollern; one grandson, the apothecary Balthasar Mayer (1779–1849), established the Mayer name in the region. Balthasar’s son Eduard Mayer (1814–1881) later moved to Pforzheim, which became the centre of the family’s activities.
Eduard and his wife Bonaventura Braun had seven children who would all, through founding and marriage, create a cross-border jewellery network in Germany and Switzerland.
Pforzheim branches
Victor Mayer (founded 1890)
Victor Mayer (1857–1946) founded a jewellery and enamel manufacture in Pforzheim in 1890. During the Jugendstil period the firm produced enamelled jewellery and belt buckles, often based on designs by artists such as Anton Krautheimer of the Munich Secession. The workshop became known for technical virtuosity in guilloché engraving and fire enamel, skills that would later underpin its work for Fabergé. Hi daughter Maria Anna Mayer
(1898-1976) would eventually take over leadership of the company together with her husband Edmund Mohr and her brother Oscar Mayer (1895-1969). Followed by his son Hubert Mayer and Maria¨s son Herbert Mohr-Mayer.
From the 1920s the company began producing Fabergé jewellery under licence, and until 1988 it manufactured pieces for Fabergé & Cie in Paris, signed Fabergé Paris. In the late 20th century, under Herbert Mohr-Mayer and Marcus Oliver Mohr, the firm became an official Fabergé workmaster and produced limited-edition Fabergé eggs and jewellery.
Meyle & Mayer (founded 1887)
Meyle & Mayer was founded in 1887 by jeweller Gustav Meyle (1846–1932) and goldsmith Julius Mayer (1856–1940), one of Eduard’s sons. The company became one of the principal producers of German Jugendstil jewellery, specialising in plique-à-jour dragonflies, enamelled portrait medallions and sinuous floral motifs, generally in gilded 900 or 800 silver.
Several works by Meyle & Mayer – including silver plique-à-jour lockets with mirrors and dragonfly pendants – are catalogued in Fritz Falk’s monograph on Pforzheim Art Nouveau jewellery and are represented in the collection of the Schmuckmuseum Pforzheim. Meyle & Mayer pieces continue to attract collectors; enamelled brooches and pendants regularly achieve mid-three- to mid-four-figure prices at design and jewellery auctions.
Gustav Meyle married Friederike Mayer (1853–1902), sister of Julius and Victor, creating a double alliance between the Meyle and Mayer families.
Swiss branches
Albert Mayer, Davos (from the 1870s)
Albert Mayer (born 11 June 1854 in Pforzheim) was the first member of the large Pforzheim Mayer family to settle in Switzerland. As a teenager he developed tuberculosis, and before turning eighteen he was sent to Alexander Spengler¨s new Sanatorium in Davos, whose high-altitude climate was becoming known for lung cures. While recovering, he lived near what later became the busy resort centre of Davos-Platz. Best known from Thomas Mann The Magic Mountain, describing Europe´s upper class in a Davos Tuberculosis retreat hotel.
By the 1880s, Davos had transformed into a major international health resort. Albert’s six siblings—already active in the jewellery and watch trade in Pforzheim—visited him frequently during this period. Seeing the constant flow of affluent British, Dutch and German visitors, the family realised that Davos offered a promising market for jewellery, watches and small luxury goods. Encouraged by this, Albert began selling items informally, and soon opened a dedicated shop.
A photograph from the 1890s shows his storefront “Albert Mayer, Juwelier” in the Davos Centralhof, on today’s Promenade 74, Davos-Platz, beside the ski-workshop of winter-sports pioneer Tobias Branger. The location placed him at the heart of the resort, serving long-stay tuberculosis patients and early winter tourists drawn to Davos’s skating rinks, sledging tracks and Alpine hotels.
Albert Mayer never married and left no descendants, but within the Mayer family his Davos venture is remembered as the first Swiss foothold that later inspired other branches—such as Roman Mayer in Territet–Montreux (from 1888) and Leicht-Mayer in Lucerne (from c. 1898)—to establish themselves in Swiss resort towns. He later opened his own hotel and jewellery shop in Davos.
Leicht-Mayer, Lucerne (c. 1898–1950s)
In Lucerne, the firm Leicht-Mayer (also E. Leicht-Mayer & Cie and later E. Leicht-Mayer & Co. S.A.) emerged around the turn of the century. Lucerne commercial records list “Emil Leicht-Mayer, Albert Mayer’s Erbe” circa 1898–1904 and E. Leicht-Mayer & Cie from 1904, registered as a retailer of watches, gold and silver goods.
The principal jeweller Emil Leicht married Anna Mayer (born 1863), a sister of Victor, Julius and Roman. Another Mayer sibling, Rudolf Mayer (1851–before 1908), married Josephine Leicht, forming a rare double marriage alliance between the families. Surviving watches show that Leicht-Mayer worked with some of the most prestigious Swiss manufacturers:
* Ulysse Nardin pocket watches in 14- or 18-carat gold, double-signed E. Leicht-Mayer & Cie, Lucerne, including minute repeater chronographs made around 1910;
* a rare Audemars Piguet white-gold digital dress watch retailed by E. Leicht, Mayer & Co, Lucerne, sold at auction in Geneva in 1990;
* 1930s silver repeaters and mid-century 17-jewel Incabloc wristwatches signed E. Leicht-Mayer & Co. Lucerne.
These pieces place Leicht-Mayer among the upper tier of Swiss jeweller–retailers of the period.
Roman Mayer, Montreux (from 1888)
The Montreux branch, Roman Mayer, forms a long-lived Swiss arm of the dynasty. Roman Mayer (1859–1911), born in Pforzheim, moved to Switzerland in the 1880s. On 19 September 1888 he opened his first watch and jewellery shop under the arcades of the Grand Hôtel Territet on the shores of Lake Geneva, a resort frequented by an international clientele including Empress Elisabeth “Sissi” of Austria.
From this base, Roman and his sons built a small network of boutiques in Swiss resorts and spa towns. Over time the family operated or was associated with shops in Territet–Montreux, Vulpera, St. Moritz, Zermatt, Interlaken, Arosa, Crans-Montana and Lausanne. In 1922 a new shop opened near the casino in Montreux; the present-day boutique on Avenue du Casino 39 traces its origin to this expansion and has remained there for more than a century.
Today the firm Roman Mayer continues to trade as a retailer of luxury watches and jewellery, representing brands such as Patek Philippe, Omega and others, and is managed by the Christidis–Mayer family as a third- and fourth-generation business.
Olympic and international roles
Roman Mayer’s son Albert Mayer  (1890–1968) followed his father into the jewellery trade in Montreux while also pursuing an international sporting and political career. He served as president of the international bobsleigh federation FIBT (1930–1960), became a member of the International Olympic Committee in 1946 and held the office of mayor (Syndic) of Montreux in several terms between 1947 and 1960.
Albert’s brother Otto Mayer (1900–1970) served as Chancellor of the IOC and co-managed the family jewellery business, illustrating how the Montreux branch linked luxury retail with the institutional world of the modern Olympic movement.
According to the Roman Mayer firm’s own history, for the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games the Pforzheim manufacture Victor Mayer – described as part of the same family – produced medals and objects decorated with Olympic rings, indicating cooperation between the German and Swiss branches of the dynasty.
Notable members
Notable members of the dynasty include:
* Victor Mayer (1857–1946), founder of the Pforzheim jewellery manufacture Victor Mayer
* Julius Mayer (1856–1940), co-founder of Meyle & Mayer
* Gustav Meyle (1846–1932), co-founder of Meyle & Mayer
* Anna Mayer (b. 1863), co-founder of Leicht-Mayer through her marriage to Emil Leicht
* Rudolf Mayer (1851–before 1908), associated with the Leicht family through marriage
* Roman Mayer (1859–1911), founder of the Montreux jewellery house Roman Mayer
* Albert Mayer (1854), founder Roman Mayer Jewelry and a Hotel in Davos
* Ida Mayer (1891–1981) jewelry company Colet
* Albert Mayer (1890–1968), jeweller, mayor of Montreux, IOC member
* Otto Mayer (1900–1970), IOC Chancellor
* Else Mayer (1891–1962), founder of the Catholic women’s order Erlöserbund
* Herbert Mohr-Mayer (b. 1933), director of Victor Mayer and Fabergé workmaster
* Manfred Mohr (b. 1938), pioneer of computer-generated art
* Wolfgang Mayer, gemstone dealer active in Bogotá and Pforzheim
* Marcus Oliver Mohr, creative director and managing partner of Victor Mayer
* Philipp Mohr, architect and designer
* Bernhard Mohr and Monika Mohr, associated with jewellery manufacturing, Teno and others, in Pforzheim
Companies
Companies founded or shaped by the Mayer jewellery dynasty include:
* Victor Mayer GmbH & Co. KG – Pforzheim jewellery manufacture (founded 1890)
* Meyle & Mayer – Pforzheim Jugendstil enamel jewellery (founded 1887)
* Leicht-Mayer – Lucerne jeweller and watch retailer (c. 1898–mid-20th century)
* Roman Mayer – Montreux jeweller with multiple Swiss resort branches (from 1888)
